- **CRT memcpy tail dispatch uses a negative index and was lifted wrongly** [documented, superseded] The CRT memcpy and memmove finish their last 0 to 3 bytes through a table indexed by a negative number, which the bounds-check pattern does not match. It is lifted as RECOMP_ITAIL to some other function, so the copy silently never happens and a crash comes much later on data that was never written. Every MSVC title that links the CRT memcpy has at least two. The v0.13.0 changelog reports a fix (#140) for the same symptom, a CRT memcpy unaligned-byte dispatch that silently skipped the copy; whether it covers the negative-index form is not stated. A manual memmove override is the documented workaround. *How:* grep -n 'RECOMP_ITAIL(MEM32(.* \* 4 + 0x' generated *.c (made at install time, not in the repository)
- **MechAssault CRT memcpy copies came back with ESP one byte off** [documented, historical] A switch arm's resync left misaligned decodes inside it: an inc esp was lifted from the middle of a real mov. Every 28 to 31 byte copy returned with ESP a byte off. Fixed in toolkit PR #135, shipped in v0.13.0.
- **Jump tables named by their last slot lost every arm after the table** [documented, historical] Jump tables were measured as one entry when named by their last slot, so memmove's backward tail lost every arm after the table, epilogue included. Fixed in PR #134, shipped in v0.13.0.
- **pushad and popad were TODO comments before v0.13.0** [documented, historical] pushad and popad emitted only TODOs, so a routine that saved every register returned with its caller's registers clobbered. Fixed in #167 (v0.13.0).
- **Failed ICALL to a caller-cleans function popped its arguments twice** [documented, historical] On a failed indirect call to a function whose caller removes the arguments, the failure path rewound over the arguments and then the caller's add esp, N removed them again. Fixed in #169 (v0.13.0). Keep the failure path to popping only the dummy return address.
- **lahf is lifted; unordered x87 and SSE compares set ZF PF CF** [documented, historical] lahf was lifted before v0.13.0. Unordered x87 and SSE compares were setting the greater-than result rather than ZF, PF and CF. Fixed in #150.
- **All eight SSE compare predicates and 4-lane reciprocal ops lifted** [documented] The v0.13.0 lifter handles all eight CMPPS and CMPSS predicates, 4-lane sqrtps, rsqrtps and rcpps, and bare cmps and scas (#151).
- **x87 results round to 24-bit significand under PC=24** [code-confirmed] The Xbox runs x87 at precision control 24 (the D3D default), so each arithmetic result rounds to float precision. Before #149 the lifter ignored this. The runtime macro RECOMP_FP_PC rounds results to 24 bits when bits 8 and 9 are not set. Burnout 3's sorted draw list froze at the start line because a value compared against its float-stored copy never settled. — generated recomp_types.h (made at install time, not in the repository):282
- **sub_XXXXXXXX_enter hook runs on every call in the manual file** [documented] Defining sub_XXXXXXXX_enter in recomp_manual.c runs it at the top of the generated function on every call, direct calls included. Added in PR #168 for tracing without replacing the body.
- **Regeneration erases hand patches; keep a checklist** [documented] Every regeneration overwrites hand edits to gen files. Patches fall into four kinds: #if 0 around crashing functions, vtable guard insertions, jump-table replacements where pattern matching failed, and extern declarations for shared globals. Keep a list and re-apply it after each run; Burnout 3 had more than 10 patch sites across 8 files.
- **stc, clc and cmc were lifted to TODO comments** [code-confirmed, historical] The conformance harness found that stc, clc and cmc lifted to /* TODO */, so the carry a following adc or sbb read kept whatever the last arithmetic left in it. MSVC emits these around multi-word arithmetic and the return-a-bool-in-CF idiom.
- **fxch st(i) was a silent no-op** [code-confirmed, historical] Capstone reports fxch with both operands (st0 and st(i)); other x87 forms carry only the explicit register. The handler read operand 0, got st0 and emitted a swap of st0 with itself, so every fxch did nothing in every title. Found by the conformance suite.
- **fnstsw ax did not model TOP and wrote only AH** [code-confirmed, historical] The x87 status word carries TOP in bits 11 to 13, which land in AH bits 3 to 5. The model stores TOP in g_fp_top, but fnstsw did not include it and the ax form wrote only AH instead of all of AX. Reads taken while the x87 stack was non-empty disagreed with hardware.
- **fnstsw did not set C2, so NaN compares looked not-equal** [code-confirmed, historical] An x87 compare against a NaN sets C3, C2 and C0 together. The CRT tests for NaN with fucompp, fnstsw ax, test ah,0x44 and jp. Before the fix, fnstsw did not model C2, so every float classification reported not-unordered and took the wrong branch. Crimson Skies' float classification exposed it.
- **js and jns evaluated the sign at 32 bits, not at operand width** [code-confirmed, historical] SF is the sign bit at the operand's width. test dl,dl; jns asks about bit 7, but the lifted condition tested the zero-extended byte as an int32, so values 0x80 to 0xFF always looked positive. cmp has the same width problem because it must truncate the difference before taking its sign. Found by a corpus function that /O2 unrolls into test and jns.
- **Flag state follows control flow, not address order** [code-confirmed] FunctionTranslator used to thread cmp and test state from one block to the next in address order, which is only right for fall-through. Optimised code lets a jcc consume a compare from a non-adjacent block. Flag state now propagates along predecessor edges, and only when every predecessor agrees; otherwise the block gets no inherited state and falls back.
- **bt, btr, bts and btc were unhandled; 386 instructions in real code** [code-confirmed, historical] The bt family lifted to a comment, so the bit was silently left alone. Real Xbox code contains 386 of them. Found when the corpus started lifting the CRT float-to-int helper, which uses btr to clear a rounding-control bit of the x87 control word.
- **rep movs on the hardware aperture must not use host memcpy** [documented, historical] Host memcpy uses vector loads that skip the element-sized accesses trapped device memory needs. rep movs touching the hardware aperture was routed through host memcpy until PR #170 (v0.13.0).
- **Generated code stores compare operands in _fa/_fb and tests them with macros** [code-confirmed] The MA2 generated code does not keep a flags register. Each instruction writes its operands to _fa and _fb (unsigned) and _fas and _fbs (signed, width-cast), then a condition macro such as TEST_Z(_fa, _fb) reads them. The comment after each line names the source instruction. The register-model doc's CMP_GE style is the older description. — generated recomp_0000.c (made at install time, not in the repository):85
- **cmp and test pattern-match to CMP_* and TEST_* macros** [documented, superseded] The original lifter design matched cmp or test followed by jcc, and emitted a C comparison with signedness handled by CMP_GE, CMP_B, CMP_L and TEST_Z. Sub-register access uses LO8, HI8, LO16 and SET_LO8 style macros that preserve the other bytes.
- **Guest registers are thread-local in the current runtime, not plain globals** [code-confirmed] The MA2 recomp_types.h declares eax, ecx, edx, esp, ebx, esi and edi as RECOMP_TLS (__declspec(thread) under MSVC). The reason given: guest threads now run on real host threads, so each needs its own register set. Thread-local access costs an indirection per use. Manual code must include recomp_types.h, or it writes a different variable. *How:* Debugger: take the TLS address first with r? @$t1 = &mygame!g_esp; dwo and poi differ for 32-bit guest values — generated recomp_types.h (made at install time, not in the repository):160
- **Register model doc: plain globals, ebp local, shown by example** [documented, superseded] The register-model doc describes eax, ecx, edx and esp as plain globals, ebx, esi and edi as callee-saved globals, ebp as a per-function local for FPO, and g_seh_ebp as the one bridge. The rules are still right, but the TLS change and the g_ebp publishing in the current tree (see tc-register-ebp-published) make the doc incomplete.
- **MA2 generated code publishes ebp to g_ebp for frameless callees** [code-confirmed] Each function in the MA2 gen code writes its local ebp to a thread-local g_ebp (about 32,500 g_ebp = ebp lines) and reads it back where a frameless callee needs the caller's frame (about 11,100 ebp = g_ebp lines, commented 'frameless: caller's frame'). This is a deviation from the docs' rule that ebp is purely local. Changing how ebp is handled affects every FPO function. — generated recomp_0000.c (made at install time, not in the repository):900
- **g_seh_ebp bridges ebp between __SEH_prolog and its caller** [code-confirmed] __SEH_prolog computes the caller's ebp and writes it to g_seh_ebp, and the caller reads it back after the call. __SEH_epilog reads g_seh_ebp on entry and writes it before returning. In the MA2 tree the lifted code writes g_seh_ebp = ebp about 38,600 times, so the bridge is in common use. — generated recomp_types.h (made at install time, not in the repository):194
- **__SEH_prolog VA 0x00244784 is a Burnout 3 address, not MA2** [code-confirmed, superseded] The SEH docs give __SEH_prolog at 0x00244784 and __SEH_epilog at 0x00244797. Those are Burnout 3 VAs. The MA2 functions index has no entry at either address, so do not reuse them. Find the MA2 CRT helper by its code pattern (frame setup that pushes a handler and reads fs:[0]).
- **Exception frames are built on the guest stack and linked from fs:[0]** [code-confirmed, open-question] The MA2 generated code builds a registration frame for SEH functions: it pushes try level 0xFFFFFFFF, a handler, and a scope table, then links it by reading the old head from fs:[0] and storing esp into fs:[0]. The docs say these frames are never walked for dispatch, so the chain is kept for stack layout and not for exception delivery. Whether a title's __try handler is ever run from this chain is still open. — generated recomp_0000.c (made at install time, not in the repository):902
- **SEH emulation for vtable calls was never implemented** [documented] The docs list full SEH emulation, wrapping ICALL in __try and __except, as not implemented. Corrupted vtables are instead handled by the centralized VA range check and per-function guards. A corrupted vtable on real hardware is caught by SEH and execution continues at __except; the port skips the call.
- **VEH allocates zero pages for NV2A MMIO at 0xFD000000 and up** [documented] Game code reads NV2A registers at 0xFD000000 and up. Windows does not map those, so the access faults. A vectored handler (AddVectoredExceptionHandler with priority 1) commits a 4 KB page there with VirtualAlloc and resumes the instruction, so reads return 0. Allocating the page only prevents the crash; a spin-wait on the zero value still loops forever.
- **Never handle divide-by-zero in the VEH: it breaks the game's own SEH** [documented] Several game functions divide by values that can be zero on purpose and rely on their __except block. A VEH that skipped the faulting instruction and returned a bogus result pre-empted that handler. The rule: a VEH may only handle faults the game cannot legitimately produce, such as NV2A register faults at addresses the port itself invented.
- **RECOMP_ICALL: manual override, then generated table, then kernel bridge** [code-confirmed] Every indirect call pushes the return address and then goes through three lookups in order: recomp_lookup_manual (hand-written overrides first), recomp_lookup (the sorted generated dispatch table, binary search), and recomp_lookup_kernel (synthetic 0xFE000000+ thunk VAs). If none match, the failure path pops the dummy return address, sets eax to 0 and logs the miss. The table is still a binary search, not a flat array; a flat-array change is in progress in the Microsoft-comparison work. — generated recomp_types.h (made at install time, not in the repository):1060
- **ICALL code range comes from mapped sections, not a fixed 0x00400000** [code-confirmed] The docs give the garbage-VA check as the fixed range [0x00400000, 0xFE000000), which was right for one title only. The MA2 runtime tests RECOMP_ICALL_IS_CODE against g_xbox_code_lo and g_xbox_code_hi, filled from the executable sections the memory layout actually mapped. Targets at 0xFE000000 and up (kernel thunks) are always allowed. Zero hi means not loaded yet, so the check allows everything. — generated recomp_types.h (made at install time, not in the repository):126
- **Calls push the real guest return address; docs show a dummy value** `000120A1`, `0001CF40` [code-confirmed] Current generated code pushes the real guest return address (the VA of the instruction after the call) and then calls. Writes through a mirror went unseen by the base view until the layout was switched to file mapping.

- **Kernel data exports live in a 4 KB area at 0x00740000** [documented] Data exports are placed in a 4 KB block at 0x00740000 holding XboxHardwareInfo, XboxKrnlVersion (the example build is 5849) and the KeTickCount counter, which a background thread refreshes from GetTickCount. The data area is what the thunk entry points to.
- **Kernel bridges read arguments from g_esp and return in g_eax** [documented] After the ICALL pops the dummy return address, arguments are at g_esp + 4n (STACK_ARG). A bridge translates Xbox pointers with XBOX_TO_NATIVE, calls the Win32 equivalent, writes the result to g_eax and returns. Xbox kernel exports are stdcall, so the callee-side bridge must not pop its arguments again.
- **Every kernel bridge must set g_eax before returning** [documented] The caller reads eax after a kernel call. A bridge that forgets to set g_eax leaves a stale value from an earlier call. NTSTATUS functions return 0 for success, and allocation functions return a pointer.
- **NT pseudo-handles like NtCurrentThread are -2, which must be sign-extended** [documented] NtCurrentThread is (HANDLE)-2, or 0xFFFFFFFE as a 32-bit value. Widened as unsigned on a 64-bit host it no longer matches Windows' -2, so DuplicateHandle failed and the CRT retried forever. Handle tokens from 0xFFFFFFF0 up are sign-extended in bridge_resolve_handle. The fix shipped in v0.13.0.
- **STATUS_CONFLICTING_ADDRESSES must map to 487 so the CRT heap grows elsewhere** [documented] When NtAllocateVirtualMemory refuses a base, it answers 0xC0000018. Windows maps that to ERROR_INVALID_ADDRESS (487), and 487 is the only error on which the MSVC CRT heap tries another address. Mapping it to the generic 317 stops the heap from growing. Both status tables carry the 487 mapping since v0.13.0.
- **Kernel call counters must be 64-bit, or logging runs on every call** [documented] A title that polls the clock through the kernel passes 2^31 calls within minutes. An int counter wrapped negative, so the log budget test count <= budget logged every call and frame rate fell to about 1 FPS. The counter is long long now.
- **Opt-in kernel switches for memory reclaim and guest synchronisation** [documented] RECOMP_HEAP_RECLAIM makes NtFreeVirtualMemory and MmFreeContiguousMemory really free and zeroes decommitted pages. RECOMP_EXT_VMA honours reservations at a fixed address above the RAM mirrors. RECOMP_TITLE_KEVENTS turns a KEVENT the title built into a host event, and RECOMP_GUEST_LOCK runs one guest thread at a time. All are off by default.

The 147 figure is the Burnout 3 import count. Use the MA2 import table for the number that matters.
- **Titles that probe the AC97 codec can skip their whole engine init** [documented] A title that links the XDK DirectSound checks the AC'97 codec. When DirectSoundCreate fails, the title skips its whole engine init, not just sound, and then never draws. Wreckless did exactly this. RECOMP_AC97_READY=1 reports the codec ready and routes the APU aperture to the emulated APU; if behaviour changes with it, the probe was the gate.
- **HAL and kernel bridges are mostly simple stand-ins** [documented, historical] Burnout 3 bridged about 68 of 147 kernel imports with real behaviour, stubbed about 79 to return success (threading, audio, network, crypto) and left about 20 unused in play. The table of categories says memory uses a bump allocator, file I/O maps to CreateFileA and related Win32 calls, and NV2A push-buffer functions are stubbed.
- **NV2A spin-wait functions must be stubbed whole, not just the register read** [documented] A push-buffer function such as one that loops while MEM32(0xFD003210) & 0x100 is set never ends if the register reads zero. Mapping the page only prevents the crash. Find the function in recomp_0xxx.c, wrap it in #if 0, and add a no-op in recomp_manual.c. The same applies to D3D8LTCG push-buffer flushes.
- **NV2A translation covers register combiners, vertex microcode, textures and PGRAPH** [documented] xbox_nv2a holds the NV2A register handlers (regs from xemu) and the PGRAPH to D3D11 translation. The v0.13.0 release added vertex programs, register combiners, four texture stages, visibility reports, near-plane clipping, bilinear filtering and a threaded rasteriser. The gap analysis lists the 8-stage combiner and vertex microcode translation as done.
- **P8 palette textures are expanded to BGRA using the stage palette** [documented] P8 textures are expanded to BGRA at upload through the texture stage's palette, and dev_SetPalette re-bakes any P8 texture bound to that stage, so animated palettes work. Since v0.13.0 they sample through the stage palette.
- **A title that runs but never draws: find the probe that failed** [documented] Symptom: vblank and DPCs fire and threads run, but no frame reaches the screen and a later wait never returns. The usual cause is a device the title probed at boot and found missing, so it skipped everything that depended on it. Use RECOMP_AC97_READY, RECOMP_NV2A_TRACE, RECOMP_PB_EXEC and RECOMP_WATCHDOG_SECS to find which probe failed. A shim that makes a wait return without making the event happen usually just moves the stall.
- **NV2A trace and pushbuffer executor switches** [documented] RECOMP_NV2A_TRACE=1 shows whether the DMA_PUT register moves at all. RECOMP_PB_EXEC=1 actually consumes the pushbuffer, which the NV2A does not do by default. Without RECOMP_PB_EXEC, a D3D callback driven by a GPU interrupt (swap, fence, notifier) never fires, because nothing raises that interrupt.
- **RECOMP_WATCH and RECOMP_UNIMPL_TRAP locate writers and untranslated code** [documented] RECOMP_WATCH=<va> names the guest code that writes a value, for example a callback table slot or a ready flag. RECOMP_UNIMPL_TRAP=1 stops at the first untranslated instruction that is actually reached, rather than letting it fall through.
- **RECOMP_WATCHDOG_SECS dumps registers and the guest stack when progress stops** [documented] RECOMP_WATCHDOG_SECS=N dumps the guest registers, PUT and GET and the guest stack when the title stops making progress for N seconds. The dump names the wait the title is stuck .
- **Reading guest state in cdb: take the TLS address first** [documented] Guest registers are thread-local, so dwo(&module!g_esp) fails. Switch to the thread first, then use r? @$t1 = &mygame!g_esp and r @$t0 = poi(mygame!g_xbox_mem_offset), then .printf with dwo(@$t1). Guest memory is at poi(g_xbox_mem_offset) plus the guest address. Host registers such as @ecx are not guest registers. *How:* ~Ns (switch thread), r? @$t1 = &mygame!g_esp, r @$t0 = poi(mygame!g_xbox_mem_offset),printf 'guest esp=%08x' dwo(@$t1)
- **Crash address ranges point to the likely cause** `00010000` [documented] 0x00000000 to 0x0000FFFF is a null dereference. 0x00010000 to 0x00780000 is valid Xbox image range, usually an uninitialised global. 0x00780000 to 0x00F80000 is stack. 0x00F80000 to 0x04000000 is heap. 0x80000000 and up is kernel memory. 0xFD000000 and up is NV2A (needs the VEH). 0xCDCDCDCD and 0xDDDDDDDD are MSVC debug fills.
- **Crashes after hours of play are a stack leak; watch g_esp over time** [documented] A game that runs for half an hour and then crashes is almost always leaking simulated stack from failed ICALLs. A healthy run oscillates within a narrow range around each call. Log g_esp every N frames; a steady downward trend is the leak.
- **Native stack overflow comes from recursive ICALL dispatch** [documented] An access violation far below the stack base usually means function A calls B through an indirect call and B calls A, and each dispatch uses native stack, not the simulated one. Raise the native stack size in the linker or stub one function in the cycle.
- **Debug loop: read the ICALL trace, find the caller, read the generated C, fix minimally** [documented] The loop is: run and let it crash; check the ICALL trace for a garbage target; find the calling function with the .map file; read its generated C; check which globals it needs and whether they were set; apply the smallest fix (stub, guard, initialise a global or override); rebuild. Keep a log of each crash, its root cause and the fix, because a few root causes account for most crashes.
- **Launch from a drive-letter path: Git Bash paths break asset loading** [documented] From Git Bash, cd /e/burnout3 sets a Unix-style path, and the Windows game then fails to find its asset files. Launch with a Windows drive path (cd) so the working directory is right.
- **Build with /MAP and map native return addresses back to sub_ names** [documented] The MSVC linker .map file maps native addresses in the built exe to recomp function names. Subtract the image base from a crash or _ReturnAddress value, then look it up in the map. This is how a failed ICALL is traced back to its caller. *How:* cmake --build build --config Release -- /p:MapFile=true
- **Rate-limit diagnostics: first N, then every Kth** [documented] Logging every ICALL, kernel call or memory access produces gigabytes. The pattern is: log when count <= 5 or count is a multiple of 1000. Counters that feed the test must not overflow to negative, or every call is logged.
- **Conformance: the host CPU is the oracle for lifted instructions** [documented] The conformance harness runs the original x86 bytes on the real CPU and the lifted C on the same inputs, then compares results. Because Xbox code is 32-bit x86 and a 32-bit MSVC process is available on Windows, there is no model to disagree with. A lifted instruction can still agree while doing nothing, so comment-only lifts are reported separately.
- **Conformance snippets: MSVC __asm blocks, lifted with lift_basic_block** [documented] Each snippet is assembly text emitted as an MSVC __asm block between nop markers, compiled with /FAc. The bytes are read back from the .cod listing and lifted with lift_basic_block, not lift_instruction, because the cmp+jcc peephole lives at block level. Inputs cluster on 0x7F, 0x80, 0xFF, 0x7FFF, 0x8000 and 0x80000000 to expose width bugs.
- **Conformance corpus: linked MSVC functions lifted through FunctionTranslator** [documented] Corpus functions are compiled with /O2 /GS- /arch:IA32, linked into a DLL at a fixed base with relocations stripped, then lifted out of the linked image through the real FunctionTranslator and run against the compiled originals. Callees are lifted too, and any undefined reference fails the run. This is how the flag-propagation and js width bugs were found.
- **Conformance phase three runs a real title's functions under quarantine** [documented] Given an XBE you own, phase three maps it where it was linked, calls its functions with supplied arguments, and compares the lifted C with the real run. Only functions ending in a plain ret (not ret N), with no indirect branch, fs access, string op or privileged instruction, are comparable. A harness crash quarantines the function and reruns. On Burnout 3 the comparable set rose from 17 to 37 once callees were followed.
- **Conformance results: Burnout 3 and Blood Wake clean; Crimson Skies has two open** [documented] Burnout 3: 37 comparable functions, 161 vectors, 0 mismatches. Blood Wake: 39 comparable, 44 vectors, 0 mismatches. Crimson Skies: 35 comparable, 227 vectors, 2 functions still diverging and not yet explained (one writes a scratch byte, one returns a different value).
- **Conformance commands: snippets, corpus, XBE and filters** [documented] py -3 -m tools.conformance runs everything. --only snippets runs the GCC snippet phase. -k NAME filters to one family. --keep keeps the generated C for reading. --xbe PATH runs phase three on a title. tools/conformance/mkxbe.py builds a small synthetic XBE to exercise phase three without a game. *How:* py -3 -m tools.conformance --only snippets; py -3 -m tools.conformance --xbe tools/conformance/test.xbe
- **Two Docker images because 32-bit MSVC link hangs and Rosetta cannot run 32-bit** [documented] The amd64 image compiles and links the corpus in seconds, but link.exe never finishes under 32-bit emulation. The i386 image runs the 32-bit harnesses, but Rosetta cannot execute 32-bit x86, so the harness cannot run on the amd64 image. A 32-bit PE built on one image runs on the other unchanged. Corpus and XBE phases need the real MSVC, not GCC, because GCC would test codegen no title contains.
- **vsdownload needs --accept-license; the MSVC toolchain is not redistributable** [documented] The ISC licence covers the msvc-wine scripts, not the Visual Studio toolchain they download. vsdownload.py fetches it from Microsoft only under the licence you accept with --accept-license. Neither Docker image should be pushed to a shared registry.
- **Conformance starts both sides from identical register, x87 and stack state** [documented] Four things had to be equalised: every GPR is zeroed before the call (an indirect call lets eax be cleared), st(0) is given the same value on both sides, the x87 control word is the model's value, and both stacks are filled with 0xCD so an uninitialised local faults on poison instead of disagreeing. Without these, the harness reported convincing false failures.
- **Full test run: 630 passed and 0 skipped with a C compiler on PATH** [documented] The unit suite is py -3 -m pytest tools/. Tests that compile the lifter's output skip rather than fail when no C compiler is on PATH, so check the skip count. The clean v0.13.0 run is 630 passed and 0 skipped, plus 5,843 conformance vectors with no mismatches. For clang installed but not on PATH, export it under Git Bash. *How:* py -3 -m pytest tools/ (on Git Bash: export PATH=/c/Program Files/LLVM/bin:$PATH)
- **tools.split writes per-function .s files with the bytes as data** [documented] For decompiling by hand, tools.split writes one .s file per function with the original bytes as db and the disassembly as comments, because x86 mnemonics do not uniquely determine an encoding. The file assembles to the shipped bytes by construction. On the Xbox Dashboard's text, 2,254 of 2,254 functions matched byte for byte. A function is deleted once its C matches.
- **run_ghidra.sh is the one-command naming pass; decompile is optional and slow** [documented] XBE=/path/default.xbe tools/ghidra_naming/run_ghidra.sh runs extract, analyse and export without decompilation. Then py -3 tools/ghidra_naming/merge_names.py previews the names. run_ghidra.sh decompile N decompiles up to N functions per run and resumes; decompile all takes hours. *How:* XBE=game/default.xbe tools/ghidra_naming/run_ghidra.sh; py -3 tools/ghidra_naming/merge_names.py
- **Build the .exe from the game project, not from the toolkit** [documented] The toolkit's CMake builds only libraries. The game project's CMakeLists adds the toolkit with add_subdirectory, globs generated *.c (made at install time, not in the repository) and links the xboxrecomp umbrella target, and it sets /bigobj and /LARGEADDRESSAWARE. Building the toolkit's CMakeLists gives libraries and no exe. *How:* cmake -S. -B build && cmake --build build --config Release (from the game project)
- **Six runtime static libraries; the umbrella target links them all** [documented] kit/source/game/src/ builds six static libraries: xbox_kernel (kernel), xbox_d3d8 (D3D8 to D3D11), xbox_dsound (DirectSound mixer), xbox_apu (MCPX APU from xemu), xbox_nv2a (NV2A from xemu plus custom) and xbox_input (XInput). The runtime builds with GCC on Linux since #172.
- **Microsoft's x86 path emits one flat code arena; ours emits real C functions** [documented] Microsoft's PowerPC path maps guest functions to host functions with real call and ret. Its x86 path emits one flat arena of code, with guest control flow as jmp and entry only by guest-derived addresses, and about 99 percent of .text lies in a handful of huge host functions. xboxrecomp emits real C functions with call and ret, so function boundaries matter and must be found, which is why the detection work above exists.
- **Flat directly indexed dispatch is in progress; ours is still a binary search** [documented, open-question] Microsoft resolves indirect branches with one indexed load from a flat table. Our dispatch runs up to three lookups, one of which is a binary search over about 8,900 entries in translator.py. Replacing it with a bounds check and a flat array indexed by va minus code base (about 8 bytes per byte of code span) is marked in progress.
- **Adopted from the Microsoft study: real return address and indirect-target feedback** [documented] Two items from the Ficl/Fission study landed: pushing the real guest return address (commit 7fbcc79), and indirect-branch target feedback (commits e4e95a7, 10277e9, 19a2ec8, d06af63). Also landed: decoding direct call targets the sweep stepped over (fd71a0e). Rejected: block-granular entry points, full block threading, materialised flag booleans and register-to-host mapping.
- **The guest XBE can be read out of a BC package's SVOD container** [documented] Microsoft's BC packages hold the guest XBE inside an SVOD container. The container is readable, which lets the coverage oracle compare our function detection against the donor title's own byte-dense address map. The reader is tested on synthetic data only, and no extracted XBE is committed.
- **Kernel ordinal mapping is XDK-specific, so the runtime cannot be shared as-is** [documented] Burnout 3 (XDK 5849) expects a different kernel export ordinal mapping than Halo (3911) and Crimson Skies (5659). The toolkit's tools/ were reconciled, but the kernel routing cannot be shared as a swap; the per-title ordinal data is a separate gate.
- **lookup.py class: registered class to vtables and slots** [code-confirmed] python lookup.py class NAME [-n MAXSLOTS] takes a registered class name (exact first, then substring) and prints its parent, descriptor, class-id global, create and constructor functions, then each vtable with its slots. Each slot line shows the slot number, offset, target VA, a header hint (category, calling convention, parameters, returns) and up to 3 strings. Verified: lookup.py class MAMech resolves to vtable 00469CD0 with 162 slots. *How:* cd ''; python lookup.py class MAMech -n 8
- **lookup.py vt: vtable address (or an address inside it) to its class** [code-confirmed] python lookup.py vt ADDR takes a vtable start, or any address inside one, and prints the owning class, how it was determined (getter, anon, embedded), and the slots. Use it on a vtable address read from a constructor or from memory at runtime to learn which class it is. *How:* python lookup.py vt 0x469CD0
- **lookup.py fn: a function's vtable slots, hint, strings, callers and pointer refs** [code-confirmed] python lookup.py fn ADDR shows every vtable slot holding that function (vtable, class, slot number and offset), the header hint, the strings it references, its callers, and the places that refer to it by pointer, capped at 20. A function that no vtable holds and no caller reaches is a seed candidate. *How:* python lookup.py fn 0x1087C8
- **lookup.py str: regex over strings, returning the functions that use them** `0012F52F` [code-confirmed] python lookup.py str REGEX is case-insensitive and lists each function whose referenced strings match, with the strings, the header hint and up to two owning vtable slots. Verified: lookup.py str ^Waypoint returns 4 functions, including 0012F52F (the Waypoint vtable method, slot 4 of 0046FEC8, class MAWaypoint). *How:* python lookup.py str Waypoint
- **classes.tsv kinds: registry, rtti, named vtable, anonymous vtable** [documented] classes.tsv has one row per class with a kind: registry (215 classes from the runtime class registry), rtti (8 std:exception descriptors only), named_vtable (a vtable whose slot returns a display name such as Default POV Behavior) and anon_vtable (no name; the note gives constructor functions and the host class). Use the kind to decide how much to trust a class name.
- **How the MA2 class registry is read from descriptors** [documented] A class descriptor D holds a runtime class id at +0, the value -1 at +4, the create function at +0xC, the name at +0x24 and the parent name at +0x28, found in the registration function sub_B4C60. The name lives in the next 0x30-byte block after the create function, so earlier scans that paired name and create in one block were off by one class. Each entity class's get-descriptor slot (slot 21 for entities, slot 6 for behaviours) links its vtable to the class, and the class-id global receives the id at startup.
- **re_index limits: vtables need a code reference and 3 or more pointers** [documented] A vtable is only found if some code references its address and at least three function pointers follow. About 900 anonymous tables are secondary or this-adjusted tables, or helper classes. Parent classes beyond the registry (MoeEntity, MAEntity) have no record, so lookups for them return nothing.
- **q.py prints string addresses with their xrefs from ma2.xbe** [code-confirmed] q.py loads ma2.xbe with inspect_xbe.Xbe, builds a table of printable strings over the data sections and an xref map from idx.pkl. Each argument is a regex; it prints each matching string's VA with the functions that reference it. Both the Xbe path and the bringup path are hard-coded to a typical machine, so edit them before running elsewhere. *How:* python q.py 'Waypoint'
- **lookup.py reads index.pkl while q.py reads idx.pkl** [code-confirmed, open-question] The re_index folder holds index.pkl (read by lookup.py) and idx.pkl (read by q.py). Rebuild both with build_index.py, which needs capstone. If only one pickle is rebuilt, the two tools may disagree (inferred from the file layout).
- **xemu GDB stub: launch with -s and talk RSP on port 1234** [documented] xemu.exe -s opens a GDB remote-protocol stub on localhost:1234, and -S pauses at start for attaching before boot. Commands used by the docs: g reads registers, m and M read and write memory, Z0 and z0 set and remove software breakpoints, c continues, s single-steps, and a raw 0x03 halts the guest. *How:* xemu.exe -s (then connect to localhost:1234 with the RSP packet format)
- **xemu: halt before setting breakpoints, always remove them, keep halts short** [documented] The GDB stub times out if breakpoints are set while the guest runs, so halt first. A leftover int3 crashes the game, so remove breakpoints in a finally block. The whole emulated system freezes during a halt, so keep halts under about 2 seconds.
- **Hash each 4 KB page of 0x10000 to 0x560000 in xemu, let the player drive for a few seconds, hash again and dif** `004DB000`, `004D9000`, `00549000`, `0040F000` [documented] Hash each 4 KB page of 0x10000 to 0x560000 in xemu, let the player drive for a few seconds, hash again and diff. On Burnout 3, 47 of 1520 pages changed in three seconds of driving, mostly 0x4DB000 to 0x4E0000 (physics), with 0x4D9000 (camera), 0x549000 (part transforms) and 0x40F000 (vehicle state) also active. These are Burnout 3 values; they show the method, not MA2 addresses.
- **Find floats and 4x4 transforms by value and shape in a memory dump** [documented] Search changed pages for floats near a value you can see (a car speed from position deltas). A world transform has row 3 column 3 equal to 1.0, column 3 rows 0 to 2 equal to 0.0, rotation rows of length about 1.0, and translation in row 3. These checks narrow a changed page to the object transform.
- **D3D8 is gone from modern Windows, and Xbox D3D8 is not PC D3D8** [documented] Xbox games call Direct3D 8, which the modern Windows SDK does not ship. Xbox D3D8 also adds push buffers, tiled memory and NV2A-specific features that PC D3D8 lacks, so the translator must emulate both the API and the GPU semantics. The v0.13.0 translator maps the real XDK format constants from kit/source/game/src/d3d/d3d8_xbox.h
- **D3D8 objects are fake COM vtables that route to D3D11** [documented] Each Xbox D3D8 object (device, vertex buffer, texture, surface) is a struct whose first member is the interface pointer, pointing at a static vtable of function pointers. Game code calls methods by vtable offset, so call [eax+0x88] is SetRenderState (slot 34). The single device is a static instance in the translator.
- **Fixed-function D3D8 state is emulated with a few HLSL shaders** [documented] The D3D8 texture stage state (COLOROP, COLORARG and ALPHAOP) is turned into a pixel shader flag set, so D3DTOP_MODULATE means texture times vertex colour. MODULATE is the common case in Burnout 3, where it carries baked ambient occlusion. Only the combinations a game uses are implemented; COLOROP alone has 25 values.
- **Xbox texture formats map to DXGI; swizzled and odd formats convert at upload** [documented] DXT1, DXT3 and DXT5 map to BC1, BC2 and BC3. A8R8G8B8 maps to B8G8R8A8, D24X8 to D24_UNORM_S8_UINT and D32 to D32_FLOAT. Swizzled Xbox textures are unswizzled at upload, and formats with no DXGI equivalent (YUY2, P8, bump formats with odd channel order) are converted in software first. The XDK packed binary values are in d3d8_xbox.h.
- **Vertex buffer Lock returns a system-memory shadow; Unlock uploads it** [documented] Lock hands out a pointer into a system-memory shadow copy and Unlock updates the GPU buffer from it, through UpdateSubresource or a staging Map. Writes made by the game while locked appear in the shadow, so the upload has to happen at Unlock, not at each write.
- **DrawPrimitiveUP copies into a 4 MB dynamic ring buffer** [documented] D3D8 DrawPrimitiveUP draws from a client pointer with no vertex buffer, and D3D11 has no equivalent. The translator copies the data into a dynamic buffer with MAP_WRITE_DISCARD and draws from it. The v0.13.0 release describes this as a 4 MB ring buffer.
- **FVF texture-coordinate count and size come from bit fields** [documented] The texcoord set count is bits 8 to 11 of the FVF. Each set's component count is the 2-bit D3DFVF_TEXCOORDSIZE field at bits 16 plus 2 times the set index, where 0 means 2 components. Sets map to R32_FLOAT, R32G32_FLOAT, R32G32B32_FLOAT or R32G32B32A32_FLOAT, and the vertex shader declares every texcoord as float4.
- **D3D8LTCG device context is a static object reached through a global pointer** `0035FB48`, `0035D6A0` [documented] In Burnout 3's D3D8LTCG section, the device context is a static object inside the D3D section, not heap-allocated, and a global pointer (0x35FB48) points at it. Key offsets include the push buffer cursor at +0, render target at +0x784, viewport at +0xEE0, and the 64-byte render-state block at +0xCA0. Capture 16 KB from xemu and load it at boot, with pointers fixed up. These are Burnout 3 values.
- **D3D8LTCG render-state flush has several entry points; stub the mid-entries** `0034D410`, `0034D530`, `0034F5B0`, `003558A0` [documented] One ~80 KB Burnout 3 function flushes render state to the push buffer and has four entry points (0x34D410 full, 0x34D530 standard, 0x34F5B0 partial, 0x3558A0 minimal) that share one end address. The docs suggest stubbing the mid-entries to return the current write pointer, and overriding the standard entry to capture output. These are Burnout 3 addresses.
- **Present pumps window messages then calls IDXGISwapChain Present with vsync** [documented] The present path drains the Windows message queue with PeekMessage (exiting on WM_QUIT) and then calls IDXGISwapChain:Present(1, 0). It replaces the game's own Present call from the rendering loop.
- **State objects are cached by descriptor** [documented] D3D11 blend, rasterizer and depth-stencil objects are costly to create, so the translator caches them keyed by their descriptor and reuses a match. The docs' simplified cache is a 64-entry array with memcmp on the descriptor.
- **Push buffer creation returns success; spin-waits stay stubbed** [documented] Push-buffer creation functions are stubbed to return success, and tiled render targets are stubbed because D3D11 handles render targets. Any function that spin-waits on NV2A registers must be stubbed whole, because a VEH page only stops the access fault.
- **Shared vtable methods carry the owning class in their generated name** [documented] With --names, rtti writes a name map that merge_names --apply consumes, so generated functions read CBaseEntity__000162C2 instead of sub_000162C2. Method names are not recovered, only the address and owning class.
- **tools.xiso is the recommended extractor for disc images** [documented] The disc-image doc recommends tools.xiso, shipped in-tree, and lists xdvdfs and extract-xiso as alternatives. Extract the whole tree so default.xbe and every data file are present; the XBE parser needs only the header.
- **Easy recomp targets: RenderWare, single-threaded, standard D3D8, offline** [documented] The root README rates an easier target as RenderWare or another known engine, single-threaded, using standard D3D8 calls, with a small .text section, offline only and no PC port. Harder ones are custom engines, multi-threaded code, push-buffer microcode, LTCG-heavy binaries, Xbox Live dependence, or a good PC port already existing.
- **Gap analysis status: PGRAPH and push-buffer replay were added from Burnout 3** [documented, historical] The gap analysis against xemu lists NV2A register access and VEH-based MMIO as done, push-buffer parsing as a stub, and PGRAPH to D3D11 and push-buffer replay as added from the Burnout 3 code. It rates texture-format coverage and cube and volume textures as partial.
- **Contributors add a conformance case when a lift is fixed** [documented] The README asks every lifter fix to come with a conformance case, so a regression is caught by execution rather than by a text comparison. Unit tests that match the emitted text only show that the output changed, not that it is correct.

<a id="t09_bringup_history"></a>

## Bring-up history: controller, tank physics, audio, movies and stability findings

## Bring-up history

Findings from the early bring-up of the PC build (controller bridge, rumble timing, tank physics timing, HRTF option, movies, save and checkpoint behaviour, crash analyses). Items marked `superseded` were corrected later; the later entry wins.


### Facts

- **A clean exit code does not prove a run passed** [code-confirmed] The v19 M09b interaction was reported failed even though the process exited 0. The first recorded graphics error was CreateTexture2D (depth) with HRESULT 0x887A0005, followed by failed framebuffer readbacks. Acceptance must come from the log content, not from the exit code. *How:* Read the run log for graphics errors and readback failures before accepting any game run.
- **Device-loss recovery is tested with process-local injected loss only** [verified-in-game] The source gpu_failure path used to mark the device failed for good. The recovery work in v21 retries creation under a bounded deadline and passes the four native recovery fixtures. The v21 recovery is an injected loss inside the process, not a real driver reset, so the original NVIDIA failure cause remains open. *How:* Run the four regression fixtures hardware_device_recovery, hardware_device_recovery_exhaustion, hardware_gpu and enhanced_texture_matching; they finish in about 19 s.
- **Recovery verification has its own progress deadline** [code-confirmed] The recovery reviewer required a VERIFYING-state progress deadline that is checked at boundaries even when there is no presentation target. Only S_OK results count as progress, and the verification clock is suspended while the window is occluded or minimized. *How:* Covered by the recovery zero-presentation and exhaustion regression tests.
- **Controlled in-game recovery run passed on Mission09b** [verified-in-game] A bounded probe ran Mission09b at 1920x1080 with two process-local injected losses, each with two failed creation attempts. Recovery produced generations 2 and 3, expected six error lines and zero unexpected GPU errors, and exited 0 in 96 s. Player movement after recovery was confirmed, but the probe does not clear the real NVIDIA failure. *How:* probe_gpu_recovery.py with the Mission09b override; the default path does not create a device.
- **The PERF label 'GPU draws ms/frame' is CPU wall time** [code-confirmed] The PERF value labelled 'GPU draws ms/frame' is CPU QPC wall time measured around raster_batch. It includes preparation, driver time and blocking, not GPU execution. The one-shot GPU query hook flushes and waits up to five seconds, so it must be excluded from pacing comparisons. *How:* Do not read the PERF GPU draw number as GPU time; use a timestamp query for GPU time.
- **ImGui Win32 backend polls XInput every frame** [code-confirmed] The vendored ImGui Win32 UpdateGamepads polls XInput controller 0 on every NewFrame with no NavEnableGamepad gate. v21 ShowFPS called it on the presentation thread. The accepted fix is a backend-scoped IMGUI_IMPL_WIN32_DISABLE_GAMEPAD compile definition in the game CMake, which dropped the fixture counts from 25 GetState and 3 capability calls to 0 and 0. *How:* Check the game CMake for IMGUI_IMPL_WIN32_DISABLE_GAMEPAD before adding new ImGui overlays.
- **ImGui caches controller presence at init** [code-confirmed, open-question] The vendored backend caches HasGamepad at initialization and refreshes it only in its WM_DEVICECHANGE handler. The active frontend does not forward messages to ImGui's WndProc. If the controller connects after the HUD initialized, the cached absence can suppress polling, so late-connect slowdowns may have another cause. *How:* A late controller connect needs its own test; the cached-absent and late-connect cases are in the fixture.
- **OS window clamp overwrote the selected render size** [verified-in-game] On this 96-DPI desktop with a 3840x1600 primary monitor, a requested 2160 client needs 2199 outer pixels, but the 39 px non-client area and the clamp gave an actual 2141 client height. WM_SIZE overwrote the selected render_size with the OS-clamped scene extent. The fix keeps the selected render size, updates only the display, and makes startup DPI-aware. *How:* Check that a selected 3840x2160 setting persists after the clamp and that a new 2560x1440 Apply writes its INI values.
- **Selected resolution is kept; aspect is automatic** [documented] The chosen contract keeps the conventional selected resolution and an automatic aspect. Documentation that said the client size drives the scene was out of date and was corrected in the proposed copy. Scene resolution and presentation aspect are kept separate. *How:* Do not reintroduce client-driven scene sizing when changing window code.
- **Iris Xe laptop run recorded settings and exit** [verified-in-game] A v21 run on the LG Gram i7-1260P with Iris Xe (FLB100, 16 GiB) ran for 523 s and exited 0 with no timeout, logging no graphics failures. The scene was 1280x720 with a 960x720 aftermovie and a 2560x1600 fullscreen client, with original textures, draw distance 50, VSync off, uncapped frames and ShowFPS on. The run shows no compatibility pass. *How:* Segment the PERF data by menu and gameplay phase before comparing averages.
- **Packaged v15 M16 sample at 3840x2160** [verified-in-game, historical] The packaged v15 M16 sample ran at an actual 3840x2160 scene and measured 157.57 to 164.94 FPS with a maximum p99 of 8.504 ms, with world ticks advancing at the original distance. It is a 20-second sample on an older hash and is not a whole-game performance claim. *How:* Use only as an older-hash reference point.
- **Stability run ended early at 1041 s with a resolution mismatch** [verified-in-game, historical] The requested 3840x2160 window produced a 3840x2141 scene. Raw acceptance stayed false. *How:* Do not count this run as a stability pass.
- **MASaveGame.wdf is an allocated but empty WDB container** [code-confirmed] The baseline MASaveGame.wdf is 3145728 bytes long, has 30 nonzero bytes with the last at offset 67, and all bytes after offset 128 are zero. Its header begins 32 62 64 77 00 20 00 00. The initial-save container CRC is 0x67910643 with an empty body. That makes it a valid initialized container, not a serialized checkpoint payload. *How:* Use this as the expected initial state when checking whether a checkpoint wrote data.
- **Campaign profile envelope fields** [code-confirmed] In the 308-byte profile envelope, the current, highest and last-advanced destination 1 are stored under active difficulty 0. Flags3 do not include checkpoint bit 4, and the completion byte is zero. Profile offset +98 holds the saved checkpoint's campaign destination, and controller+10 is the campaign mode/state; controller+14 is the destination. *How:* Read these offsets when verifying progression from a copied profile.
- **Campaign transition 1691FB and its completion bytes** `001691FB`, `00169094` [code-confirmed] Function 1691FB separates the current destinations (+60, +6C, +78), the highest unlocked destinations (+64, +70, +7C) and the completion bytes (+68, +74, +80). The active-difficulty completion byte is set only after the 169094 check, which cannot advance past the 41 authored destinations. The completion byte alone is not the end of the game; the observer must also see the ending transition. *How:* End-to-end acceptance must include the ending transition and the completion byte, not only the final objective.
- **Final campaign record order** [code-confirmed] In the Mission01b record table the final gameplay record Mission17b is record 38, Cinema_5_5 is record 39 and Cinema_5_6 is record 40. The ending path must therefore cross those cinema records before completion is set. *How:* Use these record numbers when tracing the final sequence.
- **Mission01b salvage truck UID and target dummy** [code-confirmed] The actual salvage truck in Mission01b is UID 129492, while the target dummy is UID 129519. W2 parsed all 1715 Mission01b records. Earlier routes that targeted the dummy were wrong. *How:* Use UID 129492 when checking the salvage objective.
- **Objective4 commit flag at +0x54** [verified-in-game] Objective4 is committed when the byte at +0x54 is 1. The run that stopped on death before commit showed no dependency24 flag and no Objective4 commit. Objectives 0, 1, 2, 3 and 6 were committed before death and then reset. *How:* Check +0x54 and dependency24 before counting an objective as done.
- **Post-Raptor checkpoint action 132158 is gated by timer 132371** [code-confirmed, open-question] The authored Mission01b checkpoint action 132158 is gated by the disabled timer 132371 that follows the Raptor cinema. *How:* Reach the Raptor cinema before testing the post-Raptor checkpoint.
- **Checkpoint serialization is unproven; initial save only is verified** `0015CED6`, `00167B25`, `000B9400`, `0015EFF2` [code-confirmed] Only the initial campaign save and destination 1 / checkpoint 0 resume are verified. Checkpoint serialization and restoration are not, and the checkpoint container was still empty in the reviewed runs. The save path goes through the 15CED6 wrapper, the 167B25 begin/graph/end sequence and the B9400 writer. Save acceptance requires a populated checkpoint body, metadata and a successful fresh normal Continue, not just a writer return value. *How:* Accept a checkpoint only after a fresh-process Continue has loaded it.
- **Condition consumer 165E0 / 1695D4 sets phase 3** `000165E0`, `001695D4` [code-confirmed] The successful condition consumer at 165E0 and 1695D4 sets phase 3 and conditionally clears profile bit 4. A callback store alone is not enough to explain a phase change. The generated branches match the original in the audit, and no translation bug was found there. *How:* Trace this consumer when investigating why a checkpoint flag is not cleared.
- **Timer and objective differential oracle results** [code-confirmed] The timer and objective differential oracle recorded 1884 matches against original Xbox code, comprising 1600 timer cases and 284 objective cases, with no mismatches. It was built with MSVC /O2 /fp:precise /std:c11. Callback 1452D4 and the pre-evaluation at 163ABC are intercepted matching boundaries, so the oracle supports arithmetic and gates, not full mission correctness. *How:* Rerun the oracle after changing generated mission code.
- **DropPack ownership callback 1452D4 audit** `001452D4` [code-confirmed] The DropPack callback 1452D4 was checked with 986 unique inputs and 1010 invocations, with no mismatches against original code. Ownership suppression runs before the force and fired steps. Physical pickup, player binding and real vehicle transitions were not tested, and the fixture covers virtual receiver and teardown only. *How:* Physical pickup needs a human test.
- **Authored DropPack is the Explosive Pack, not Mission01b salvage** [code-confirmed] The authored DropPack in the mission data is the Explosive Pack, which is armed and triggered manually under DropPackManager. The Mission01b salvage objective uses MAPowerUp instead. Testing salvage therefore cannot validate the 1452D4 callback. *How:* Use the Explosive Pack to test DropPack detonation and vehicle transitions.
- **Shoreline trigger 130832 and barge set** [code-confirmed] Trigger 130832 is a LogicType 1 OR of wall 130103 and barge damage 133083. The barge set 130700 targets 129604 and 129605. The latest v28 private profile metadata could not prove that Mission01b was reached before the Raptor cinema. *How:* Reach Mission01b normally before the wall or barge trigger when testing shoreline behaviour.
- **Three shoreline cutscene tanks: UIDs and cinema** `00132557`, `00132555`, `00132500`, `00133496` [code-confirmed] The three-shoreline group consists of raptor jack UIDs 132557, 132555 and 132500, all using template 40026. They are started by trigger 130832 with TLraptorstart and MACinema 41226. The initial pair 133496 and 133503 belongs to a different cinema, 132026, so it does not explain the three-tank symptom. *How:* Check the UIDs when identifying which tanks a test is observing.
- **Tank spring integration 1718ED is elapsed-time based** `001718ED`, `00170D91`, `00170C08`, `0010A3DA` [verified-in-game] 1718ED (MATank slot 27) integrates the spring and suspension using elapsed time, and the original runs it at 30 Hz. 170D91 is the normal refresh and 170C08 is the int-to-float step that feeds the wheel 170FD8. The accepted universal fix sets the spring to original 30 Hz timing and fixes the normal refresh; it is not a level-specific or frame-cap patch. *How:* Any change to tank physics must preserve the 30 Hz semantics and be checked at 60, 144 and uncapped rates.
- **Whole-tank 30 Hz wrapper 109536 was rejected** `00109536`, `00109FF4` [verified-in-game, superseded] 109536 is the MATank whole-actor update (slot 7). The spring-only candidate 8DF1 gave smooth aim but excessive acceleration and pitch, so it was also rejected. *How:* Enable with Try-Tank-Physics.cmd only; the normal Start path keeps it off.
- **Shoreline tanks level after build BA6C** `001718ED`, `00170D91` [verified-in-game] The confirmed in play that the three shoreline tanks now level correctly in build BA6C, which carries the universal spring and normal refresh fix. Excessive pitch and wheelie at uncapped frame rates stayed open and was reopened, so whole-tank physics is not complete. *How:* Use the BA6C-era tank code as the baseline for further physics work.
- **Tank mouse aim is routed through 1753E6** `0017537D`, `001753E6`, `00109FF4` [verified-in-game] Generic AI yaw at 17537D is a no-op for the player tank. The authored tank function 1753E6 takes arg4 and passes it through 109FF4 to the inline yaw at 488, which is where mouse X now reaches. Hull arguments 1 to 3 are preserved. The human test confirmed the horizontal aim works. *How:* Mouse-aim changes should be made at 1753E6 and not at the generic 17537D.
- **Stolen tank player override is not yet traced** `00172967` [documented, open-question] The player-override path around 172967 was still untraced at the last report. *How:* Trace the stolen-player path before changing aim for vehicles.
- **Rumble: request timing, duplicate suppression and expiry** `0001FE60` [code-confirmed] The earlier 9.5 s guest-silence claim is withdrawn: duplicate guest requests are suppressed and the suppressed count is printed only at the next transition. The original effect expiry is a one-shot at gen0001 sub 1FE60, and the original 5000 ms cap with continuous effects refutes a 500 ms watchdog as safe. The accepted D666 candidate keeps the authored stop retry and reserves ten slots, with the zero-discard deferred while the same port has an active effect. *How:* Do not add a blanket watchdog; match the original one-shot expiry.
- **Pause and focus stop rumble through an authoritative signal** `0001FE60` [code-confirmed] The pause path needs an authoritative pause signal because host-side policy alone was not enough in 20 fixture cases. The accepted candidate adds a pause entry to gen1FE60 on top of the D666 expiry and an atomic pause suppression in xinput_device, while leaving the original completions and resumes intact. The original pause was a one-shot zero that was lost while the old slots resumed. *How:* Physical pause and focus tests are still needed.
- **Kernel timers used a 15-16 ms clock** [code-confirmed] GetTickCount64 advances in 15 to 16 ms steps, and the kernel_bridge due time used it. A period request alone therefore does not give 1 ms deadlines. The accepted timer fix uses a QPC origin with safe 100 ns conversion, a 1 ms high-resolution wait cleanup, and arms the event under lock before publishing it. The periodic phase catch-up redesign was deferred. *How:* Use QPC for new deadlines in kernel_bridge rather than GetTickCount64.
- **XInput feedback is initialized once before first output** [code-confirmed] The rumble callback policy uses an INIT_ONCE XInput setup before the first non-silent output, and an atomic front-end callback publish with SRW locking. A regression must show that the first output leads to a pause without InputInit having run. The candidate passed 33 checks in each of two runs, while the old build failed 16 in each. *How:* Use the rumble test that runs output before InputInit.
- **Controller inversion and vibration bridge mapping** `0021F989`, `00223DBC` [verified-in-game] The native bridge had its UI rows swapped. Inversion is guest +0x76 with mask 1 (bit 0) and vibration is guest +0x75 with mask 2 (bit 1); the older text saying bit 1 and bit 2 was superseded. The base bridge at 21F989 bypassed the derived accept at 223DBC, which applies the active camera before persistence. *How:* Do not change axis negation; the fix is in the bridge mapping.
- **Name entry: MAKeyboardDlg callers and text capture** `0048C2F8`, `00224D27`, `001FB975`, `0048F7D0` [code-confirmed] The name entry is reached from Avatar_locker 48C2F8 with action 224D27 going to 1FB975 with flags 82, which opens MAKeyboardDlg 48F7D0. The modal hit failure came from a record offset that was empty, and the keyboard text is captured while the physical pad keeps working. ReadMouse ignored the text-capture gate and was fixed in the same change. Keyboard WM_CHAR does not suppress GetAsyncKeyState, so a separate suppression is needed. *How:* Check the text-capture gate in both keyboard and mouse input when adding dialogs.
- **Prompt text candidate for controller bindings** [code-confirmed] The prompt candidate B8499A99 changes 31 of the 181 authored rows, all in controller or menu text, and keeps the original baseline 80A2C005. It corrects the 'lore pull' corruption and the D-pad and stick wording and keeps the hack sequences unchanged. The ABXY and bare-press prompts were checked against the authored strings. *How:* Compare prompt text against the 181-row baseline before changing it.
- **QTE HUD drawing hook at 1FE68D** `001FE68D`, `001FF94C`, `000C1640`, `000C0FD0` [code-confirmed] The QTE HUD draw for the jacking button is function 1FE68D, with the hook at 1FE6B2 after the original visibility and texture gates. The text path uses UTF-16 font routines at 1FF94C, C1640 and C0FD0. The original QTE glyphs are baked into state artwork, and the 2820-check oracle with 786 original-code records found no mismatch. *How:* The hook lives in gen/recomp_0053.c; keep the original gates before any label drawing.
- **QTE captions were rejected by the tree-rect check** [code-confirmed] At 3840x1600, the LT and RT QTE icons were rejected by the tree-rect check, because the root 2 assumption in 76D4 treated a zero-area structural container as invalid. The accepted fix 81B49 and CB12 keeps the original root no-paint callbacks in place. The ABXY caption rows 191, 195, 199 and 203 were replaced with current-binding captions. *How:* The original structural container is valid; do not require a non-zero rect.
- **KBM QTE mouse icons were swapped and are now fixed** [verified-in-game] The KBM QTE showed Mouse2/RMB on the left and Mouse1/LMB on the right, which was wrong for the PC mapping. The fix exchanged the render rect and legend for rows 207 to 214 so that the plate, highlight and binding move together. The confirmed in play in build B63B that the mouse order is correct. *How:* Change icon placement only through the render rect and legend exchange, not by swapping labels.
- **KBM QTE gets 1.25x response time** `0018F27B` [code-confirmed] The QTE step timer gives keyboard and mouse a 1.25x response window while the controller keeps the original 1.0 window. The change is post-original, after the response write, and does not reset the countdown or affect the global clock. The 602-case baseline with 3010 checks matched the original authored budgets of 0.5, 0.55, 0.65 and 0.75. *How:* The mode is read from the input mode API; the controller path must not change.
- **QTE controller glyphs and labels remain partly open** [documented, open-question] Some original QTE state artwork still shows controller letters and has no letter-free replacement. The alternate-art draft was still under review for alpha and glow drift, and the LT and RT labels were still pending human acceptance. The full native QTE was not claimed as working. *How:* Check the live QTE captions by hand before claiming the LT and RT path works.
- **Enhanced FMV file layout and selection** [code-confirmed] Enhanced movies are MKV files in Movie/Enhanced/2x with the same names and frame rates as the originals. MAIntro at startup is enhanced automatically, while Attract, SPIntro and ConquestIntro follow the default Original or the enhanced option. The option is stored as PC FMV quality, default 0. The enhanced content is scaled into the guest 640x480 movie texture, so no true 2x texture is used yet. *How:* Replace a movie by putting a matching MKV in Movie/Enhanced/2x; the original BIK is the fallback.
- **BinkOpen handle mode was misread as a C string** `00390FC0` [code-confirmed] Retail BinkOpen with handle mode 0x800000 was treated as a C string in ma2_bink_opened, so the movie-open path did not handle it correctly. The fix resolves the handle to its canonical path through a read-only helper in kernel_bridge, and it only whitelists the original movie path and junctions. Movie opens in handle mode are checked before any guest pointer use. *How:* Any new movie opener must treat handle-mode values as handles, not strings.
- **enhanced_open guard fix for LastFrameNum and frame rate** [code-confirmed] The original Bink movie struct stores the public FrameRate at +0x14 and its divisor at +0x18, and the enhanced_open guard read LastFrameNum at +0x10 instead. The one-line fix sets LastFrame to 0 for rate 2997 over divisor 100 so that the canonical MKV opens with the correct timing. Before the fix the oracle had 1 failure, and after it 25 passes. *How:* The enhanced MKV must match the original 2997:100 rate and 4:3 SAR.
- **Enhanced MAIntro is played in the packaged build** [verified-in-game] In build v25 the enhanced MAIntro (778 frames at 2997:100) was selected, advanced from frame 2 to frame 4, and skipped to the title on an early Space press. Video-option persistence and the deliberate close were not tested. The earlier clean exit was a guest HalReturnToFirmware routine, not a deliberate quit. *How:* Check the Video option and deliberate quit by hand; do not count the exit code as proof.
- **USB SET_REPORT crash: invalid write after TD allocator** `0042532E`, `004253C9`, `00425264` [code-confirmed, superseded] The access violation was a write of guest FFFFFFFF from native RVA 310AF47, mapped to the original SET_REPORT setup at 4253C9 (setup word 02000921). The write landed after the TD allocator at 425264, which uses a global free head at 534D0C. *How:* Use the 0xC0000005 log entry and the RVA to find the crash site in a new run.
- **Kernel dispatch caller check fix for IRQL raise** [code-confirmed] The caller check in kernel_hal read MEM32(g_esp), but kernel_bridge had captured the TLS g_xbox_kernel_caller and then popped 4 bytes before the call. The accepted two-file candidate (kernel_bridge 17F7 and HAL 1166) makes KfRaiseIrql and KeRaiseIrqlToDpcLevel enter and leave a dispatch region with the captured caller and the saved state. The historical FFFFFFFF value was not reproduced, and the fix is not a universal crash guarantee. *How:* The IRQL raise must keep the captured caller in TLS and not re-read the stack.
- **Mission restart OOM in the guest heap** [code-confirmed] A restart load ran out of guest heap: the stderr at 122228 shows a request of 3761904 bytes against 48785136 of 50855936 in use. The generic heap tail join fix (D27) reuses freed tail blocks and was checked with 94 contracts and an independent peer review of coalescing, tombstones, alignment and locking. The actual tail geometry during the incident was not recorded. *How:* Watch the heap OOM line in the stderr when testing a restart.
- **Restart heap reuse is in the 2959 and later builds** [code-confirmed] The D27 heap tail-join change was built as a one-TU kernel archive (FEB564/4490) in which 30 of 31 members are unchanged and only the layout object differs. It was included in the combined human-test build 805659 and later. *How:* Check the restart after any kernel archive rebuild.
- **MSVC C1001 on generated units 0057, 0059 and 0097** [code-confirmed] The MSVC internal optimizer raised C1001 on the generated units gen0057, gen0059 , earlier, gen0097 after 189 of 203 steps. The workaround compiles those units with /Ob0 and keeps /O2 and the source unchanged. Native performance impact was not measured. *How:* Use the per-unit /Ob0 flag if the same C1001 returns; do not change the source.
- **Pulse laser is authored as class 7 BA template 36031** [code-confirmed] The pulse laser is authored as class 7 with type 1 (resource 31857) and a body and tip of two draws, each from a 64x64 ARGB single-mip texture. It is not class 12 mortar. *How:* Trace pulse faults from the class 7 template 36031, not the mortar class.
- **Pulse laser blend fix: constant alpha source** [verified-in-game] The renderer mapped colour and alpha blend factors together but supplied RGBA instead of a replicated alpha for the class 7 draw. For the pulse, source 8003 with alpha off and destination 1 with add equation 8006 is the case that was wrong, and the blend constant FF000000 is used. The behaviour-only constant-alpha blend change was accepted and the confirmed in play the pulse lasers are visible. Mixed constant colour and alpha is not supported and is still a documented limitation. *How:* Mixed colour and alpha blend constants are still unsupported; test those cases separately.
- **Burst and BA36031 texture inference withdrawn** [verified-in-game, superseded] The inference that BA36031 used a separate resource was withdrawn, because it shares the canonical glow textures. A 30-frame burst that ended before the 600 ms release was an invalid test. Valid tests must hold the fire input and capture at least 1.2 s. *How:* Capture at least 1.2 s of held fire when testing pulse rendering.
- **Line-width cause of invisible pulse was refuted** [verified-in-game, superseded] The point-size register NV097 0x43C is discarded by the PB/HLSL path, but the pulse does not use that path. This superseded the point-sprite causal claim. *How:* Do not add line-expansion code for the pulse.
- **Cinema1_1a is a skippable prologue; test from Mission01b** [documented] Cinema1_1a is a skippable non-gameplay prologue. The first playable mission is StreetSweeper Mission01b. Automated tests that stay in the prologue record no firing evidence, so they must reach Mission01b before arming the weapon. *How:* Use the StreetSweeper index 1 path for automated mission-1 tests.
- **HRTF audio is off by default** [verified-in-game] Try-HRTF-Audio.cmd turns it on and the normal start leaves it off. The HRTF decode path is a separate experiment and was not proven on hardware. *How:* Enable the HRTF path only with Try-HRTF-Audio.cmd.
- **Audio mix trace markers in the build** [code-confirmed] The mix and gain trace is bounded to 96 lines and enabled by the GAIN_TRACE and MIX trace settings. A build that lacks the markers MIX_TRACE, GAIN_TRACE, HRTF, [APU-MIX] or [APU-GAIN] in its EXE was a stale archive. Checking the EXE for these strings is the quick test that the trace is compiled . *How:* Search the EXE for the marker strings before reading any audio trace.
- **Audio clipping in the mission-2 battle is still open** [inferred, open-question] Battle audio hit the int16 rails from about 75 s, with submix 6, 7, 8 and 9 headroom at zero. The W4 check found that duplicate routing of bins 6 and 7 was not the cause, and that the 3D classifier threshold is not an explosion count. The actual clipping source and any audible fix remain open, and the apu_core int16 output at the battle end is a full-scale negative rail. *How:* Do not claim an audio fix without a matched human listen and a trace from the same battle.
- **Audio tail CPU budget is 128 plus 128** [code-confirmed, open-question] The audio tail path is still above its CPU budget of 128 plus 128 on the audible stream. Tail guards were not accepted; the audio work was judged on its underrun, backpressure and glitch counters, which were zero in the XA2 run. CPU tests are not proof of shipping audio quality. *How:* Check the XA2 underrun, backpressure and glitch counters in the audio test output.
- **Audio report found legal low-pitch, HRTF bypass and drain-stop bugs** [code-confirmed] The apu_vp and apu_state repairs keep guest active state, notifier, offsets, loops and ownership, and they were tested with the matching fixtures. The audible result was not proven. *How:* Look at apu_vp and apu_state before changing voice stop or filter code.
- **First explosion hitch: cold first-use is a hypothesis** [inferred, open-question] A warm relaunch does not show the first-explosion hitch, which fits a cold first-use cost, but this is not proven. The reported 5-second phase totals cannot be summed into one frame cause. *How:* Measure event-local first-use cost before optimizing.
- **Checkpoint save latency measurements** `0015EFF2`, `000B9400` [verified-in-game, open-question] The raw checkpoint call 15EFF2 took about 146 ms, with the writer B9400 taking about 145 ms and overlapping it. One profile-only run showed the graph span at 0 and 2 to 3 ms, with up to 34 uncovered callbacks. The measurement added no save optimization. *How:* Use the save timeline to attribute latency before changing kernel storage.
- **Save and Quit path 167DB6 and 167ED9** `00167DB6`, `00167ED9`, `00167B25` [code-confirmed] The Save and Quit path runs through gen0037 at 167DB6 and 167ED9, with the transfer envelopes around the checkpoint call. Probes around those two sites record the native IO order and the profile callback without double counting. The path was instrumented but not optimized. *How:* Keep native IO order and the profile callback union when adding probes.
- **Capture ZIP must be built before writers are disposed** [verified-in-game] A sharing violation came from the recorder: the writers were disposed before the ZIP was built. CaptureHost Collect and RecorderFinish now keep the writers open until Dispose and build the ZIP before the final Dispose. *How:* Use the Playthrough capture kit output; do not dispose writers before collecting the ZIP.
- **Resume checks profile_origin_sha256 instead of the exe hash** [verified-in-game] Resume originally required the exact executable hash, so it blocked the first build after ED91. It now accepts a build transition when the profile_origin_sha256 marker matches the same canonical PC Release identity. Differing packages with a mismatched origin marker are rejected, and the transition is recorded in the new run metadata. The old run, profile and latest pointer are left untouched. *How:* Use Start-Playthrough.cmd Resume to continue an existing profile after an in-place build.
- **Decision: install into the original PC Release folder in place** [documented] Builds are applied in place to the original normal-launch installation, backing up only the replaced files and never copying assets. This superseded the earlier Playtest v29-style publishing. *How:* Use the in-place installer with a strict protected-file hash check before and after.
- **In-place installer replaces the EXE last with rollback** [code-confirmed] The in-place installer renames the held old EXE and commits the new EXE last, so a failure restores the old name. It then cleans up the exact known replacement backups. An earlier attempt failed with a sharing lock error (WinError 5) and was replaced by this lock-retire-atomic mechanism, which was checked with a dummy cross-process proof. *How:* Run the installer with the reviewed runner and the grant file, and check the protected-file hashes before and after.
- **Root launcher routes to PC Release first** [code-confirmed] The root launcher (hash 4c55f308) routes to PC Release first and falls back to the build folder. PC Release MechAssault 2.exe with hash a81c93da is the authoritative normal destination. Older assumptions about the routing were superseded. *How:* Check the launcher routing before assuming which EXE runs.
- **Build identities in the history** [code-confirmed, historical] The history of EXE hashes: packaged v16 A81C93DA; v21 261D0F90; v22 A373EECB; v25 2A192D35; v26 835DF838; v27 139E9A10; v28 901A6AEF; then in-place builds 1076AFC8, ED91, 71AC, 2485, 2959CD55, 8DF1EBEB and B06E7C90. Each entry is historical once a later build is installed. Matching a hash confirms the build, not its behaviour. *How:* Record the hash of the EXE under test with every result.
- **** [documented] Before a grant, the reviewer checks that no MechAssault, mechassault2_recomp, gpu_test or ffmpeg process is running. *How:* Check the process inventory and wait for the owned child to exit before any new game launch.
- **Decision: fixes must be universal engine changes** [documented] Mission, cinema or UID specific patches, forced flattening of tilt, and frame-rate caps are not accepted. Scene or UID guards may be used only as opt-in diagnostics. *How:* Check every physics or timing fix for mission and UID specific branches before accepting it.
- **PS4 controller is supported only through XInput** [documented] The current implementation supports only XInput controllers. A PS4 controller is supported only if it exposes XInput, and native DirectInput or PS4 support is not claimed. Drivers are not installed by the project. *How:* Record the connection mode of a PS4 controller before claiming compatibility.
- **The PERF data had to separate sustained fill and overdraw from CPU submission, resource creation and sync spik** [documented, open-question] The PERF data had to separate sustained fill and overdraw from CPU submission, resource creation and sync spikes, because the GPU draw metric is CPU wall time. No blanket particle culling was accepted. *How:* Segment the explosion phases before any fix; do not cull particles to hide cost.
- **Rumble after pause and boost landing** [documented, open-question] The root gap was a focus-only feedback gate. The fix work accepts a focus policy that stops motors on pause, focus loss or close, and resumes a fresh demand, but physical controller acceptance is still pending. *How:* Physical pause, focus and close tests are still needed for rumble.
- **Protected user data set during in-place installs** [code-confirmed] Each in-place install records a strict before and after hash snapshot of the protected files, which include the enhanced movies, saves, settings, results and the root launcher. The installer reports any missing, changed or added file. An additive app-data Cache exception was accepted once, and the snapshot difference was kept as evidence. *How:* Compare the before and after snapshots after every in-place install.
- **Capture records window, focus, controller and save events** [code-confirmed] The capture recorder logs native and focus state every 500 ms (coalesced) and a committed-save timeline every 2 s, with about 144 bytes of native context, the device and 14 encoded settings. It reads the getter machine byte, data section and module base of the owned child, and it rejects unknown layouts. It does not poll XInput and does not inject input. Committed save flags 0x74 and volume values at 0x1C20 are watched, but transient guest toggles are a stated coverage gap. *How:* Read the capture ZIP timeline to see the focus, controller and save events for a session.
